subject: math
cluster: Summarize, represent, and interpret data on a single count or measurement variable
skillName: Data Plots on the Number Line
intro: There are three common ways to display a single set of numerical data on the real number line: a dot plot, a histogram, and a box plot. A dot plot stacks one dot per value, so a stack's height is the frequency of that value. A histogram groups values into equal-width intervals called bins and draws a bar whose height is the number of values in each bin (a value landing exactly on a boundary belongs to only one bin). A box plot displays the five-number summary, the minimum, first quartile $Q_1$, median, third quartile $Q_3$, and maximum, with a box from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ and whiskers to the extremes; the interquartile range is $\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$. In this lesson you will read these displays, build the five-number summary, and choose an appropriate display for a data set.

items.prompt: A dot plot of quiz scores has stacks of heights $1,3,4,2$ over the values $6,7,8,9$. How many students scored at least $8$?

steps: In a dot plot, the height of a stack is the frequency (the number of students) at that value, not the value itself.
Scoring at least $8$ means scoring $8$ or $9$, so add the stack heights over $8$ and $9$.
The stack over $8$ has height $4$ and the stack over $9$ has height $2$.
$4+2=6$ students scored at least $8$.

items.prompt: Find the five-number summary of the data set $4,7,8,8,10,12,15$.

steps: The data is already ordered from least to greatest and there are $n=7$ values.
The minimum is $4$ and the maximum is $15$.
With $7$ values the median is the $4$th value, which is $8$.
Exclude the median and use the lower half $4,7,8$; its median is $Q_1=7$.
Use the upper half $10,12,15$; its median is $Q_3=12$.
The five-number summary is minimum $4$, $Q_1=7$, median $8$, $Q_3=12$, maximum $15$.

items.prompt: For the data set $5,6,8,9,11,12,14,18$ (with $n=8$), find the five-number summary and describe the box plot.

steps: The data is ordered and there are $n=8$ values, so the median is the average of the $4$th and $5$th values: $\text{median}=\frac{9+11}{2}=10$.
The lower half is $5,6,8,9$; its median is $Q_1=\frac{6+8}{2}=7$.
The upper half is $11,12,14,18$; its median is $Q_3=\frac{12+14}{2}=13$.
The minimum is $5$ and the maximum is $18$.
On the box plot, draw the box from $Q_1=7$ to $Q_3=13$ with a line at the median $10$, then extend whiskers to the minimum $5$ and the maximum $18$.
solution.answer: minimum $5$, $Q_1=7$, median $10$, $Q_3=13$, maximum $18$; box from $7$ to $13$ with a line at $10$ and whiskers to $5$ and $18$

items.prompt: Group the data $2,4,5,7,9,11,12,14,15,19$ into bins of width $5$ starting at $0$, using the intervals $[0,5),[5,10),[10,15),[15,20)$. Give the frequency of each bin for the histogram.

steps: Each bin includes its left endpoint and excludes its right endpoint, so a value on a boundary belongs to the bin to its right.
Bin $[0,5)$ holds values from $0$ up to but not including $5$: that is $2$ and $4$, a frequency of $2$.
Bin $[5,10)$ holds $5,7,9$ (the value $5$ goes here, not in the first bin), a frequency of $3$.
Bin $[10,15)$ holds $11,12,14$ (the value $15$ does not go here), a frequency of $3$.
Bin $[15,20)$ holds $15$ and $19$, a frequency of $2$.
The bar heights of the histogram are $2,3,3,2$.

items.prompt: A box plot of a data set has minimum $12$, $Q_1=18$, median $25$, $Q_3=30$, and maximum $40$. About what fraction of the data lies between $18$ and $30$? Also find the IQR.

steps: Each of the four sections of a box plot, the two whiskers and the two halves of the box, contains about $25\%$ of the data, regardless of how long that section looks.
The values $18$ and $30$ are $Q_1$ and $Q_3$, so the region between them is the whole box.
The box runs from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ and holds about $25\%+25\%=50\%$ of the data, which is $\frac{1}{2}$.
The interquartile range is $\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1=30-18=12$.

items.prompt: A histogram of ages has bars of heights $4,7,5,2$ over the bins $[10,20),[20,30),[30,40),[40,50)$. How many people are younger than $30$?
items.hint: Younger than $30$ means the age falls in the bins $[10,20)$ or $[20,30)$. Add those two bar heights.

steps: People younger than $30$ are counted in the bins $[10,20)$ and $[20,30)$.
The bar over $[10,20)$ has height $4$ and the bar over $[20,30)$ has height $7$.
Add the two frequencies: $4+7=11$.
So $11$ people are younger than $30$.

items.prompt: Find the five-number summary of the data set $3,5,9,9,11,14,20$.
items.hint: There are $7$ values, so the median is the $4$th value. Find $Q_1$ from the three values below the median and $Q_3$ from the three values above it.

steps: The data is ordered with $n=7$ values; the minimum is $3$ and the maximum is $20$.
The median is the $4$th value, which is $9$.
The lower half (excluding the median) is $3,5,9$, so $Q_1=5$.
The upper half is $11,14,20$, so $Q_3=14$.
The five-number summary is minimum $3$, $Q_1=5$, median $9$, $Q_3=14$, maximum $20$.

items.prompt: A data set has first quartile $Q_1=23$ and third quartile $Q_3=41$. Find the interquartile range.
items.hint: The IQR is the difference between the third and first quartiles. Do not subtract the minimum from the maximum, that would be the range.

steps: The interquartile range is defined as $\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$.
Substitute the given values: $\text{IQR}=41-23$.

items.prompt: Find the median of the data set $6,8,10,13,15,19$.
items.hint: There are $6$ values, an even count, so the median is the average of the two middle values.

steps: The data is ordered and there are $n=6$ values, an even count.
The two middle values are the $3$rd and $4$th values, $10$ and $13$.
Average them: $\text{median}=\frac{10+13}{2}=\frac{23}{2}=11.5$.
The median is $11.5$.

items.prompt: A teacher has the test scores of $120$ students and wants to display the overall shape and spread of the scores. Which display is more appropriate, a dot plot or a histogram, and why?
items.hint: Think about how many dots a dot plot would need for $120$ students versus how a histogram summarizes large data into a few bars.

steps: A dot plot places one dot per data value, so $120$ scores would require $120$ stacked dots and become crowded and hard to read.
A histogram groups the scores into a few equal-width bins and draws one bar per bin, so it summarizes a large data set into a small number of bars.
Because the data set is large, the histogram clearly shows the overall shape and spread while the dot plot would be unreadable.
Therefore a histogram is the more appropriate display.
solution.answer: A histogram, because it summarizes a large data set ($120$ values) into a few bars that show the shape and spread, while a dot plot would need $120$ stacked dots and be unreadable.
